Newborn Care

After the umbilical cord falls off: caring for the healing navel

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The day the cord stump comes away can bring a new set of questions. A small mark of blood or an unfinished-looking navel is not necessarily a problem, but active bleeding, spreading redness or an unwell baby needs prompt attention.

What happens as the stump separates

The small piece of cord left after birth gradually dries, shrivels and changes from a pale or yellowish appearance to brown, grey or almost black. It may look quite different from one diaper change to the next. Those changes in the stump itself can be part of normal drying; redness spreading across the surrounding skin is a different finding.

Separation often happens around the first or second week, although some stumps take longer. There is no exact day every baby must follow. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a medical review if the stump remains attached after three weeks.

Do not pull or twist it, even when only a small piece appears to be holding it on. Let it come away naturally. Trying to speed up the final stage can disturb the healing skin and cause bleeding.

Before it falls off: clean, dry and protected from rubbing

Wash your hands before handling the area. If urine, stool or other dirt gets onto it, gently clean the soiled area with water and a clean cloth, then pat it dry. Avoid digging into the navel with a cotton bud, scraping away material or repeatedly checking underneath the stump.

Fold the front of the diaper below the stump when practical, or use a newborn diaper with space for it. Change wet or dirty diapers promptly. Choose clothing that does not rub or tightly cover the area; you do not need a particular style of outfit to achieve this.

Keep the baby comfortably warm while allowing the stump to stay dry. The dry cord itself does not have normal sensation, but the surrounding skin can be sore or inflamed. Crying when the area is touched should not be dismissed on the grounds that the cord has no nerves.

Alcohol and antiseptics are not routine aftercare

Routine rubbing alcohol is not needed for ordinary cord care. Clean, dry care is the usual recommendation; repeatedly applying alcohol, oils, powders or other preparations does not make the area heal better. Do not use household or traditional substances to encourage separation.

WHO recommends a particular chlorhexidine cord-care programme only in settings where harmful traditional applications are common. This is a specific newborn-service intervention, not a general instruction to buy an antiseptic or apply alcohol because infection is a concern.

If your maternity or newborn team has given a prescribed local cord-care plan, use exactly the product and method they specify. Do not substitute a different concentration or continue a product after separation unless instructed. A suspected infection needs medical assessment rather than stronger cleaning.

After separation, leave the healing skin alone

You may find the dried stump in the diaper or notice that it has come away during a routine change. The navel underneath may still have a small raw-looking area or a little dried blood. It does not have to look like a fully healed belly button immediately.

Keep care gentle. Clean any soiling with water, dry the area and avoid rubbing or picking at a scab. Do not try to remove every trace of dried blood. Taping a coin or a tight dressing over the navel will not improve its shape and may irritate the skin.

While the area is still wet or healing, a sponge wash can make it easier to keep it dry. Once the stump is off and the navel has healed, ordinary bathing can resume in line with your newborn-care advice. There is no universal extra number of days to wait after separation; the condition of the skin matters. Always support and supervise your baby throughout a bath.

A small spot of blood is different from active bleeding

A few drops of blood around the time the stump separates can be part of normal healing. A small mark that stops is different from blood that keeps appearing, runs from the area or soaks the diaper. Contact your baby’s clinician immediately for active or continuing bleeding.

A little clear or lightly blood-stained moisture may occur as the skin heals. Colour by itself cannot tell you that discharge is harmless. Persistent wetness, thicker pus, a foul smell or increasing redness needs assessment, especially when the baby is not feeding or behaving normally.

Avoid repeatedly lifting a scab to check for blood. If the appearance is changing and you need advice, describe whether the amount is increasing and how long it has been happening. Do not wait for a routine visit when fresh bleeding continues.

A small moist lump may be an umbilical granuloma

Sometimes a small pink, red or brownish moist lump remains after the cord separates. One possible explanation is an umbilical granuloma, an area of healing tissue that may release a little pale-yellow fluid. A clinician should confirm the cause, because a lump or persistent drainage is not always a granuloma.

Some granulomas settle; others need treatment to help the tissue dry and heal. Your clinician can explain whether observation or a particular treatment is appropriate, how the nearby skin will be protected and when the area should be reviewed again.

Do not cauterise the area or start a remedy based only on an online photograph. Tell the clinician if drainage continues, a lump changes or a new opening is visible. A bulge that becomes more obvious with crying may have a different explanation and should also be shown to the baby’s healthcare professional.

Look for infection signs in the skin and in your baby

Infection around the cord, called omphalitis, needs prompt medical care. Warning signs include redness spreading from the navel, swelling, tenderness, pus or foul-smelling discharge. Seek urgent assessment rather than trying to clean these signs away. Infection rates vary by setting, so a low percentage from a general article is not a reason to ignore symptoms.

Watch how the baby is doing too. Poor feeding, unusual irritability, marked sleepiness, difficulty waking, breathing trouble or an abnormally high or low temperature can signal illness. A temperature of 38°C or higher in a baby under three months needs urgent medical advice. A seriously unwell baby needs emergency care even without a fever.

Babies born early, with a low birth weight or with other medical needs may have an individual newborn-care plan. Follow it and ask for advice readily if the navel or the baby’s behaviour changes. You do not need to wait for several warning signs to appear together.

What to explain when you ask for help

Tell the clinician your baby’s age, when the stump fell off or whether it is still attached, what the discharge or bleeding looks like, and whether redness is spreading. Mention temperature, feeding, wet diapers and any change in alertness. Also say what products have been applied.

If you are unsure whether a small finding is normal, asking the newborn team is reasonable. Simple daily care should become easier as the skin heals. The goal is a healthy, comfortable baby and a healing navel, not making the cord separate as quickly as possible.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Clean, dry care and natural separation are the usual approach.

Routine alcohol is not needed; WHO’s chlorhexidine recommendation applies to specific settings.

Persistent drainage, active bleeding or signs of newborn illness require assessment.

How BeMama can help

Use diaper changes for a brief look at the area, and keep the newborn team’s contact details handy if something changes.

When to seek help

Seek urgent help for spreading redness, pus, continuing bleeding, poor feeding or unusual sleepiness. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical advice; a very unwell baby needs emergency care.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Umbilical cord care in newborns
  • World Health Organization — Maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience, 2022
  • World Health Organization — Caring for a newborn
  • NHS — High temperature in children

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Do not pull, pick or try to speed up separation.
  • Clean soiling gently and keep the area dry.
  • A few drops at separation differ from active bleeding.
  • Have a persistent moist lump or drainage assessed.
  • Watch your baby’s feeding and alertness as well as the navel.

Frequently asked questions

When should the stump fall off?

It often separates during the first couple of weeks, with some variation. If it remains attached after three weeks, arrange a medical review. Seek help earlier for bleeding, infection signs or an unwell baby.

Can I remove the last little piece?

No. Let it detach naturally. Pulling or twisting can disturb healing tissue and cause bleeding.

Should I use alcohol after it falls off?

Routine alcohol is not needed. Follow gentle clean, dry care unless the newborn team has prescribed a specific plan.

Is a small blood spot normal?

A few drops around separation can occur. Fresh blood that continues, repeatedly returns or soaks the diaper needs immediate advice.

Is yellow discharge always harmless?

No. A small amount of fluid can occur with healing or a granuloma, but pus, foul smell, persistent wetness or redness needs assessment. Colour alone cannot establish the cause.

Can my baby have a bath?

While the navel is still healing, sponge washing can help keep it dry. Once the stump is off and the skin has healed, follow your newborn team’s advice about normal bathing and dry the area gently.

What if a red lump remains?

It may be a granuloma, but have a clinician confirm the cause. Do not begin home cauterisation or another treatment based only on its appearance.

Does it matter if my baby has no fever?

Yes. Poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, spreading redness or other concerning changes still need attention. A newborn can be seriously unwell without fever.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
